claims.claim: Observational learning is the acquisition of information, skills, or behavior through watching the performance of others, either directly or through media such as films and videos.

The working definition of observational learning is attributed to Albert Bandura, who proposed social learning theory, the view that learning occurs through modeling, imitation, and social interaction and can happen without direct reinforcement.
Bandura described four steps that must be followed for observational learning to succeed: attention, retention, reproduction, and motivation.
Models are the people or characters we learn from; they are often parents, other adults, or other children (peers), and they may also be symbolic, such as characters in books or on television.

Vicarious reinforcement is the process whereby a person becomes more likely to perform a behavior after observing another person being reinforced for it; observing a model being punished makes imitation less likely (vicarious punishment).

Bandura's Bobo doll studies (Bandura, Ross, and Ross, 1961) are the classic historical foundation of research on observational learning: children who watched an adult act aggressively toward an inflatable Bobo doll imitated those aggressive actions, while children who watched a nonaggressive model showed less aggression.

Not everything watched is copied: imitation depends on attention, retention, and the ability to reproduce the behavior, and motivation is shaped by what happened to the model; observers may also learn a general rule rather than copy a specific act, so observational learning involves more than imitation.

The Bobo doll paradigm has drawn methodological, interpretive, and ethical critique in the research literature, including the artificiality of the laboratory setting and the availability of competing explanations for the children's behavior.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What the Bobo doll studies show about real-world aggression
positions: The classic interpretation: children who observed an adult acting aggressively toward a Bobo doll imitated those aggressive actions, evidence that aggressive behavior can be learned by watching.

Critiques in the research literature: the laboratory setting was artificial, children were deliberately frustrated and separated from their parents, and competing explanations (such as playfulness, demand characteristics, or the unusual situation) could account for the children's behavior, so the studies' reach into everyday aggression is debated.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the Bobo doll studies as the classic historical foundation of observational learning research, attributes them to Bandura, Ross, and Ross (1961), and includes the honest note that the paradigm has drawn methodological and ethical critique — without endorsing either the strongest version of the classic interpretation or the psychoanalytic alternative offered by the critics.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier A OER. openstax.org blocks direct fetch; read 2026-08-22 via an Internet Archive capture of the canonical URL (registered URL unchanged). Supports: the four steps of the modeling process as described by Bandura (attention, retention, reproduction, motivation); the three model types (live, verbal instructional, symbolic); vicarious reinforcement and vicarious punishment as changes in the observer's motivation; social learning theory as Bandura's cognitive-inclusive alternative to pure behaviorism; the Bobo doll experiment (Bandura, Ross, and Ross, 1961) as history; and the point that observational learning involves much more than imitation. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Transmission of Aggression Through Imitation of Aggressive Models (Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 63, 575-582)

sourceRecords.notes: Primary historical source for the 1961 Bobo doll experiment, used here only for the attributed history note: children watched an adult model act aggressively toward an inflatable doll, and children exposed to the aggressive model imitated those aggressive actions, while a nonaggressive model had an inhibiting effect. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
